lesson.title: The Network That Became Everyone Else's Infrastructure
lesson.summary: The internet completes this book's four historical general purpose technology case studies, and even it went through a textbook hype cycle of its own on the way to reshaping the economy.
lesson.body:
The internet is the most recent of this book's four historical General Purpose Technology case studies, and the one many readers will have lived through part of directly, tracing a path from a government research network to a genuine general purpose technology.

ARPANET, funded by the United States Department of Defense's Advanced Research Projects Agency, went live in 1969 connecting a handful of university and research computers. The TCP/IP protocol suite, standardized in the early 1980s, gave disparate networks a common language, and Tim Berners-Lee's proposal for the World Wide Web in 1989, followed by the first website in 1991, added a layer of hyperlinked, browsable documents that made the underlying network usable by non specialists. Each of those was itself a jump in capability built on the previous layer, the improvement over time test operating at the level of entire protocol stacks rather than just raw hardware speed.

Test one, broad applicability: within roughly two decades of the Web becoming publicly available, the internet had reorganized retail, publishing, banking, education, entertainment, and government services, alongside enabling entirely new categories of activity, social media, streaming, cloud computing, that had no real pre-internet analog, a breadth of applicability that rivals electricity's.

Test two, improvement over time: bandwidth, latency, and reliability improved by orders of magnitude across the decades from dial up modems to broadband to fiber and mobile networks, and each step unlocked applications the previous generation's infrastructure genuinely could not support. Video streaming, for instance, was not meaningfully possible over 1990s dial up connections no matter how good the underlying software was.

Test three, enabling new innovation, is especially clean here because so much of what the internet enabled is still actively unfolding: e-commerce logistics, cloud computing infrastructure, mobile app ecosystems, and large scale machine learning all depend on the internet as a substrate in the same layered way that modern electronics depend on the transistor. It is also worth noting honestly that the internet went through a textbook Peak of Inflated Expectations and Trough of Disillusionment of its own around the dot-com bubble discussed earlier in this book. Being a genuine GPT did not exempt it from the hype cycle. It just meant the underlying technology kept improving and finding real uses through and after the correction.

With all four historical GPT cases now on the table, steam power, electricity, the transistor, and the internet, the pattern worth carrying forward is that each took long stretches of unglamorous, capital intensive engineering work between an initial breakthrough and broad transformative impact, each showed a real productivity or adoption lag along the way, and each nonetheless clearly passed all three tests well before most observers appreciated how thoroughly it would reshape the economy around it. Whether quantum computing shares that trajectory, or belongs instead among the much larger set of technologies that generate real science but never clear the broad applicability and self-sustaining innovation bars, is the question this book turns to next, and it deserves an answer built on evidence rather than on either the boosterism of the peak or the reflexive dismissal of the trough.
